reasoning: 21-year-old female with acute onset chest pressure, dyspnea, and palpitations
Vital signs severely abnormal for age: HR 178 (tachycardia), RR 32 (tachypnea), SBP 82 (hypotension) — classic triad of shock/severe decompensation
Physical exam findings highly concerning: cool, diaphoretic skin indicates sympathetic activation and poor perfusion

Differential diagnosis includes: acute coronary syndrome (atypical but possible in young women, especially with estrogen exposure), myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, supraventricular tachycardia with hemodynamic compromise, peripartum cardiomyopathy, aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax
First-time patient with no prior records limits context but does NOT lower acuity — vital signs speak independently

Patient is alert (not ESI-1), but meets ESI-2 criteria: high-risk vital signs (hypotension + severe tachycardia + tachypnea + signs of shock) warrant immediate evaluation and monitoring, cannot safely wait

Age 21 lowers baseline concern for common causes but does not make shock vital signs acceptable; young women ARE at risk for PE (OCPs), myocarditis (viral prodrome history needed), peripartum disease, and spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD)
Requires immediate 12-lead ECG, cardiac biomarkers, imaging, IV access, and continuous monitoring — high-risk presentation
red_flags: Hypotension (SBP 82) in setting of tachycardia — suggests inadequate compensation or primary pump/vascular failure
Diaphoresis + cool skin — signs of sympathetic surge and hypoperfusion; sepsis, cardiogenic shock, or PE must be ruled out
Acute dyspnea + chest pressure + tachycardia + hypotension — life-threatening causes (ACS, PE, myocarditis, tension pneumothorax, sepsis) must be excluded
Severe tachypnea (RR 32) — suggests respiratory distress or metabolic derangement
No prior medical history available — cannot exclude pregnancy-related complications (peripartum cardiomyopathy, amniotic fluid embolism if in labor), recent illness, or drug use
